title: Classification
objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to say what a classification task is, name the features a classifier uses, and explain why a classifier can give the wrong label.

sections.title: Sorting into groups
sections.text: Classification means putting something into one of a few groups, called labels or classes. Is this photo a cat or a dog? Is this rubbish recyclable or not? Is this message kind or unkind? A program that does this is called a classifier.

sections.title: Features
sections.text: A feature is a measurable detail that helps decide the label, such as a leaf's length, a fruit's weight, or which words are in a message. A classifier only looks at its features. If an important detail is missing, it cannot use it.

sections.title: Making the decision
sections.text: Some classifiers use a rule a person wrote, like "longer than 6 cm means big leaf". Others learn where to draw the line from labelled examples. Either way, the classifier gives each new item the label that fits its features best.

sections.title: Classifiers make mistakes
sections.text: Some items are hard to sort, and a classifier can give the wrong label. A word counter does not understand that "not fun" means the opposite of "fun". Check important results, and let a person decide when it really matters.

examples.title: Example 1: Sorting leaves by one feature
examples.output:
3 small leaf
9 big leaf
4 small leaf
11 big leaf

examples.title: Example 2: Sorting messages by their words

check_questions.prompt: Which of these is a classification task?
options: Sorting photos into cat or dog
check_questions.explanation: Sorting photos into cat or dog puts each item into one of a few groups.

misconception.0: Adding gives a number, not a group.
misconception.1: Printing shows data. It does not sort it into groups.
misconception.3: Turning off a screen does not sort anything.

check_questions.explanation: 6 is not more than 6, so the else part runs and it prints small leaf.

misconception.1: > means more than, and 6 is not more than 6.
misconception.2: The program prints a label, not the length.
misconception.3: One of the two print lines always runs.

check_questions.prompt: The program from Example 2 is given the message "this was not fun". What will it say?
options: not happy, because it understands the word not
happy, because it only scores fun and ignores not
check_questions.explanation: "not" has no score, so only "fun" counts and the score is 1. The program does not understand meaning.

misconception.0: The program only adds up word scores. It does not understand not.
misconception.2: The code runs fine. It just gives the wrong label.
misconception.3: The program has no way to ask anyone. It only counts words.

try_it.title: Try It Yourself
try_it.instructions: Change the message so the program says not happy. Try using words with a score of -1.
